name: Barcelona Watch Tower (Baluarte)
history:
Currently a spot for tourists to admire the sea, the Baluarte once offered vigilance along the coast of Barcelona, Sorsogon, protecting the coastal community from possible attacks. 
 During the Spanish colonial period, the Barcelona Watchtower was constructed as part of a wider connection of fortifications that aimed to defend the settlements and monitor vessels voyaging the seas. This baluarte in Barcelona is part of the network linked with Bulusan fortifications acting as a defensive system against Moro raids during the 18th and 19th centuries. 
 This lookout structure was built for protection rather than an ornament, further proving the historical significance of the use of masonry in coastal defense. Today, its purpose has long changed, but this structure remains as an evidence of Barcelona’s pursuit of protection for the people who once settled along Barcelona’s coast.
technical_description: Situated directly across from the St. Joseph Parish Church facing the Pacific Ocean, the Baluarte was constructed in 1874 under Spanish colonial administration as an integrated coastal defense bastion and look-out post. Today, its roofless coral masonry remains unrestored but is structurally stabilized and managed by the local government unit (LGU) as an open-air historical centerpiece within the larger Barcelona Ruins Park.

name: Escuela Pia Barcelona
history:
Before its walls stood as the ruins we see now, Escuela Pia in Barcelona Sorsogon, was once a place that reflected how education was presented under the social divisions of its time. 
 Built using mixed materials of stone, sea coral, and lime masonry during the Spanish Colonial Period in the 1800s, Escuela Pia originally served as an exclusive school for the children of the Spanish and lllustrados, or referred to as the privileged and educated class. It later became known as the Stone Building during the American period, opening its doors as a public classroom for children in all walks of life, until its access was prohibited due to safety concerns.
technical_description: Constructed concurrently with the town's Spanish development in the late 1800s, this structure was built using a combination of stones, sea corals, and lime masonry to serve as an exclusive educational facility for the children of wealthy ilustrados and Spanish conquistadores. The roofless, weathering coral walls are unrestored but are structurally stabilized and maintained by the LGU as a key open-air historical attraction within the Barcelona Ruins Park.

name: La Presidencia Ruins Barcelona
history:
La Presidencia, formerly known as the "Seat of the Spanish Government" during Spanish rule, was originally a two-story building constructed in 1874. It served as the office of the gobernadorcillo, a watchtower, and a fortress against Moro pirates. An underground tunnel, built manually without machinery, was recorded to have led to the St. Joseph Church across the street to provide an escape route during attacks. This tunnel has since been sealed to prevent the theft of altar pieces from the church.

The structure served as a garrison during the Japanese occupation before being restored to its original purpose following liberation. On December 25, 1947, Typhoon Jean struck the municipality, severely damaging the Presidencia and ending its decades of service as a government facility. Subsequent storms, including Typhoon Welming in 1967 and Typhoon Sisang in 1987, further deteriorated the building into the ruins seen today. Today, the site remains one of Barcelona's main attractions.
technical_description: Constructed in 1874 in Barcelona, Sorsogon, this structure stands as a significant historical ruin reflecting Spanish colonial municipal governance and administration architecture within the municipality's heritage zone.

name: St. Joseph Church
history:
While some structures reveal strength through their sizes, some show theirs through the years they have withstood. Forming the rich historical landscape of Barcelona along with the La Presidencia and Escuela Pia, the St. Joseph Church standing across these landmarks reflects the town’s religious identity, tracing back through its history. 
	The St. Joseph Parish Church, now more widely known as the Barcelona Church, was built during the 1870s, featuring neoclassical architecture, constructed using rocks, stone, lime, and coral rocks, without modern reinforcing bars. Its construction primarily relied on local manual labor, and it now stands as one of the oldest and best-preserved heritage churches in the Bicol Region. The church underwent restoration guided by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP), and was then formally recognized in September 2020. 

In the present, Barcelona Church is still actively used to hold religious and cultural activities of Barcelona, connecting the present community to its rich cultural history.
technical_description: St. Joseph Parish Church was built in 1874 and is a one-storey church made with coral stone for its floor system and exterior walls beneath an open-gable roof of unpainted steel. Interior walls, columns, beams, and ceiling are concrete, with a concrete staircase, wooden doors, and steel window frames. Materials were consistent throughout the building and generally in good condition, with no observable interventions recorded.

name: Bulan North Central School - A
history: N/A
technical_description: The Gabaldon building of Bulan North Central School - A is a single-storey building constructed in 1936 with reinforced concrete first floor and box-gable roof clad in painted steel. Exterior and interior walls, columns, and floor structures are concrete, with steel window frames, wooden doors, and a timber-finished ceiling over a ceramic tile floor. The materials used are not fully consistent throughout the building and are not generally in good condition, though no prior interventions were observed.
feature_story: Built between 1932 and 1936 with a floor plan resembling Catanduanes Central School, this three-room layout originally featured wooden materials, Capiz windows, and a "silong" without indoor toilets. Extensive reconstructions—most recently around 202 in which the original wooden components were replaced with glass, cement, and updated split stairs alongside an added stage. While virtually no original framing remains, salvaged old timber was repurposed into furniture, and district engineers plan to restructure the building back to its traditional design using wood-pattern PVC wall tiles.

name: Bulan South Central School
history: N/A
technical_description: Bulan South Central School’s Gabaldon-type building was built in 1912 is a one-storey classroom that combines a reinforced concrete floor system with painted timber exterior walls under an open-gable, painted- steel roof. The columns, beams, and the concrete floor and staircase are concrete, while doors and windows are timber-framed and painted. Materials are consistent and structurally sound overall despite the building sustaining storm damage in the past and has undergone crack repairs and concrete patching.
feature_story: Dating back to 1912, this Gabaldon building was designed for classroom setups but suffered repeated roof and doorway damage from severe super typhoons. Although 2 to 3 quick restoration passes were made, the vulnerable wood and window materials deteriorated rapidly. To permanently fix this, a phased conversion from wood to cement restoration is scheduled by district engineers to begin in 2026.

name: Old Bulan Presidencia
history: Old Bulan Presidencia, formerly known as the Bulas Old Municipal Building, was built in 1920 and was inagurated in January 2, 1921. The structure was designed by Ar. Tomas Mapua y Bautista of the Bureau of Public Works and the first registered Filipino architect. The Presidencia is now considered as a significant cultural property under RA 10066, restored by the Philippine Government through NCP through coordination with the LGU and locals from the years 2018 to 2019. By the 15th day of April 2019, the National Historical Commision of the Philippines tuned-over the completed restoration project to Bulan LGU. The infrastructure is now converted into Bulan Heritage Museum while housing the Municipal Tourism Culture and Arts Office (MTCAO), preserving religious and historico-cultural hertiage of the municipality.
technical_description: The Old Bulan Presidencia, now the town’s heritage museum and tourism office, is a two-storey reinforced concrete infrastructure which has a combined hip and pyramid-hip roof in painted steel over painted concrete exterior and interior walls, with concrete columns, beams, and staircase throughout the building. Flooring combines ceramic tile and timber, with wooden doors and timber window frames. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, with no observable interventions recorded.
feature_story: The historic Bulan Presidencia (inaugurated in 1920s) underwent structural restoration and was officially turned over by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) on April 15, 2019.

name: San Rafael Elementary School
history: N/A
technical_description: The Gabaldon Building in San Rafael Elementary School, located in Bulan, Sorsogon, is a school property is classified under educational and Gabaldon-type structures, serving as a vital public learning facility for the local community.

name: San Ramon Elementary School
history: N/A
technical_description: In San Ramon Elementary School, a one-storey Gabaldon-type office building is situated. It has a feature of hip roof configuration that is painted over a timber exterior wall, concrete columns, and a concrete staircase supporting a timber floor system. Doors are timber and windows are steel-framed. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, with flooring previously replaced.
feature_story:
The school was estimated to be constructed around the 1930s to 1950s, with the four-corner Gabaldon Building as one of the earliest classroom buildings erected. 
Having withstood time, this Gabaldon building once became structurally unsound, which led to the conversion of its space into a storage room for the school's properties. It was recently restored in 2019, upon which the building gained back its key structural features, and returned to its original purpose.

name: Sierra Ancestral House (Casa Emilio)
history: Built in 1928, the ancestral Sierra residence stood as a pre-war hertiage home during the American colonization despite somehow having Spanish architectural features. The house was described as "aesthetically boring" due to its adapted most modern and basic features, the horizontals and verticals style, during the time. However, the purpose of this design was to withstand any climate-induced damages.
technical_description: Casa Emilio is a notable residential heritage house located in Bulan, Sorsogon, constructed in 1928. It exemplifies traditional Filipino ancestral residential architecture characteristic of the early American colonial period in the region.

name: Bulusan Belfry Tower
history: The Bulusan Belfry, traditionally called the Kampanaryo by locals, was built in the late 1700s by Franciscan friars as the largest of five defense watchtowers (baluarte de piedra) protecting the coastal settlement. Its original pyramidal dome was removed during a 1970s renovation phase; the repurposed belfry remains a structurally intact, grand symbol of Spanish colonial engineering and local resilience in Sorsogon.
technical_description: Bulusan Belfry Tower was built in 1859 as a four-storey stone masonry watchtower against pirates in the San Bernardino Strait and now serves as the church bell tower. The national government-owned structure is vacant but fully accessible. Its exterior and interior walls are unpainted stone masonry, supported by concrete columns and a concrete floor system, with a stone and steel staircase, steel doors and door frames, and concrete window frames. The painted steel roof covering has no applicable roof configuration. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, although cracks, biological growth, and mortar deterioration are present, with crack repairs and mortar repointing as past interventions.

name: Mga Moog ng Bulusan
history: The Moog Bantayan, or the historic watchtowers of the Bulusan defensive network, were constructed between the 18th and 19th centuries by Franciscan friars and local laborers to protect the strategic maritime lanes of the Embocadero (San Bernardino Strait). Today, while most of these detached coral stone towers remain in heavily weathered, roofless states, their remaining masonry foundations are preserved by local government units (LGUs) as open-air historical markers and icons of regional colonial defense.
technical_description: Mga Moog ng Bulusan is a one-storey stone masonry defense structure built in 1760 that remains in use as a defense structure. It is owned by the national government, vacant, and fully accessible, and stands beside the church and the belfry tower. The unpainted stone exterior and interior walls, stone floor, and stone staircase are open to the sky, with no applicable roof configuration. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, with only biological growth, cracks, and surface wear observed and no observable interventions recorded.

name: San Bernardino Lighthouse
history:
San Bernardino Lighthouse, historically named El Faro de Islote de San Bernardino, was designed by Guillermo Brockman in 1887. Construction was temporarily halted near the end of the Spanish colonial period, only to resume and become fully functional under American administration, a transition that accounts for the varying construction dates found across historical sources. In 1896, the lighthouse was lit for the first time using a traditional lamp and lantern to guide seafarers.

The structure holds significant historical value for both Sorsogon and the nation. Despite the treacherous waves of the San Bernardino Strait, its strategic location marked the primary maritime route into and out of Manila during the Manila-Acapulco Galleon Trade.
technical_description: San Bernardino Lighthouse is a one-storey stone masonry lighthouse built in 1893 as a navigational aid and now a cultural ecotourism landmark. It is owned by the national government, vacant, and under restricted access, with a power house and masonry storage rooms adjacent. The unpainted stone masonry walls, granite block entrances, and unpainted timber window frames sit beneath a flat roof of unpainted steel. The structure was damaged in the past by earthquake, storm, and World War II military occupation. Materials are not consistent and are not generally in good condition, with unrepaired earthquake damage and mortar deterioration observed, while past interventions include concrete patching and replacement of roof members. Data for this structure came from secondary (online) sources.

name: Casiguran East Central School
history: N/A
technical_description: Casiguran East Central School is a one-storey Gabaldon-type and government-owned property located in Casiguran, Sorsogon. It was constructed around the year 1934 with the previous and present purpose of it being a hall. The infrastructure features a hip roof configuration having concrete for its structural beams and columns members, timber for the walls and stairs, modern ceramic tiles for the flooring, and a mix of steel and wood for its roofing. Despite being not fully refurbished and is partially being renovated through the years, the infrastructure features only slight material deterioration in terms of cracks in walls, columns, beams, floor, staircase, broken glass, loose door binges, broken window glasses, door warping, peeling paint in exterior finishes, ceiling water stains and peeling paints. Beyond that, there are no other observable interventions despite 3 major renovations made.

name: Castilla East Central School
history: Tracing its roots back to around 1945, this historic building houses the library, PSDS, administrative offices, and records. The structure has undergone progressive structural updates, including fully reconstructed support columns, refreshed walling in 2018, and updated flooring works in 2026.
technical_description: Castilla East Central School, constructed in 1945, is a one-storey Gabaldon-type office and library building. It has a reinforced concrete floor system, painted concrete exterior and interior walls, concrete columns, and a box-gable roof with painted steel covering. Ceramic tile flooring, a timber-finished ceiling, and wooden doors complete the structure. Materials are consistent and generally sound, following extensive interventions including crack repairs, concrete patching, and replacement of roof, wall, column, and flooring elements.

name: Cumadcad Central School
history: N/A
technical_description: Cumadcad Central School is a one-storey Gabaldon-type building built in 1944, originally used as classrooms and now serving as an office. It is owned by the national government and stands beside other classrooms. The structure has timber floor and exterior walls painted throughout, a hip roof of painted steel, wood interior walls, concrete columns, a ceramic tile floor, and a timber ceiling, doors, and window frames. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition following a major restoration in which wall sections and flooring appear to have been replaced.
feature_story: The site features both old and new Gabaldon structures, with recent updates utilizing double-wall construction and PVC cladding alongside renovated ceiling work to support its modern function as a District Office.

name: St. John the Baptist Parish
history:
St. John the Baptist Parish Church, located in Poblacion, Castilla, Sorsogon, has a history closely associated with the establishment and development of Castilla as a town and an ecclesiastical community during the Spanish colonial period.

Castilla was organized as a town in 1827, following the transfer of its settlement center from Bulabog. Before becoming an independent parish, the town was under the ecclesiastical administration of the broader parish structure in the region. The establishment of its own parish marked an important milestone in the religious and community life of the municipality.

The church, reportedly built in 1816, is a stone structure constructed with the assistance of local residents using lime and molasses as binding materials. Despite subsequent renovations, its original walling remains largely intact. Although the façade has been finished with cement, much of the church's original structure has been preserved.

Over the years, the church sustained damage from several typhoons that affected the province. In 2009, renovation works were undertaken through the combined efforts of donors, assigned parish priests, and parishioners. During these renovations, the original roofing, which had been blown away, was replaced, and the ceiling was reconstructed using steel and fiber cement. The altar, sacristy, and function hall were also refurbished.

The parish continues to hold religious and cultural significance for the community. In honor of its patron saint, St. John the Baptist, the annual town fiesta is celebrated every June 24, coinciding with the saint's feast day.
technical_description: Saint John the Baptist Church is a one-storey religious infrastructure situated at Castilla, Sorsogon which was constructed in 1816. The property features unpainted, mixed-material exterior walls, painted concrete interior walls, brick columns, and concrete beams beneath a hip roof, with a ceramic tile floor. Doors combine wood and steel, and windows frames are steel. Materials are consistent but treated not generally in good condition, with no observable prior interventions. Also, the church also has a historical marker inaugurated on November 7, 2010.

name: Clemente Building, Donsol Comprehensive High School
history:
The Clemente Building at Donsol National Comprehensive High School (DNHCS) is a treasured pre-World War II heritage structure built in 1936. For nearly nine decades, it has stood as a symbol of the enduring legacy of education in Donsol.

It is a gabaldon-type architecture, like many 1930s school buildings in the Philippines were built under the Gabaldon Law, featuring elevated concrete floors, capiz windows, and high ceilings for ventilation. 

As a pre-war structure, it's one of the few in Donsol to predate the Japanese occupation. This building is considered a cultural marker of the American colonial period education system.
technical_description: Clemente Building is a single-storey reinforced concrete historical building originally built for educational purposes. The building is now abandoned, with unpainted concrete exterior walls, columns, beams, and floor system and no available roof configuration or covering. Steel window frames and a concrete staircase remain despite its deteriorated state. The assessed materials of the infrastructure is consistent but rated not generally in good condition, having suffered storm damages and partial removal of structural components, with some wall sections previously replaced.
feature_story:
Inside the grounds of Donsol Comprehensive National High School stands a structure that has witnessed the changes of time. Amid the busy activity of the modern school, Clemente Building remains silent in the school's changing landscape. 
The Clemente Building was constructed in 1936, serving as a classroom for many generations. Its architectural and structural features highlight the value of durable materials in construction, but more than that, they offer glimpses of its beautiful history.
The Donsol Advocates for Culture, Arts and Heritage Association Inc., along with the teachers, researchers, and residents of Donsol, seeks to petition Clemente Building Ruins to be recognized by the National Commission for Culture and Arts as one of the notable heritage sites in the Philippines. This petition aims to strengthen the preservation and protection of the historical significance of the structure.
photo: Clemente Building, Donsol Comprehensive High School

name: Donsol East Central School
history: Originally constructed in 1936 as a ground-level structure, the Gabaldon building served as a library and offices before undergoing major changes. After suffering severe storm damage to its roof, corroded "kalintipay" (Capiz) windows, decaying floors that creaked during earthquakes, and persistent 3–4 day floodings, it was almost slate for demolition. Instead, full reconstruction projects (first elevated in 1995 and rebuilt in 2012) transformed it into a multi-use hub for classrooms, evacuation, seminars, and division conferences.
technical_description: In Donsol East Central School, a one-storey Gabaldon building is being utilized as a library and office. The property has a timber flooring and box-gable roof of painted steel over a painted concrete wall. Concrete columns and staircase supports a timber floor system, with wooden doors and timber window frames all throughout. The assessed materials of the infrastructure are consistent and are generally in good condition despite past storm and flood damage, having received crack repairs and concrete patching.
feature_story:
Donsol East Central School is home to one of the oldest Gabaldon buildings in Sorsogon. 
According to Sir Alex R. Baltazar, a local, alumnus, and a current teacher and Senior Bookkeeper of the school, the Gabaldon building has stood for decades, providing a space for education to many generations including himself. Over the years, the building has undergone two restorations, where the classic gabaldon feature of "silong" has been removed, and the necessary accessibility feature such as ramps, have been added. 
As of this writing, major deterioriations are visible in the structure, with some portions of the Gabaldon being partially inaccessible and unsafe for academic utility. With this, the school faculty expresses requests for rehabilitation or restoration to maximize the building's space for academic activities.

name: Gubat Heritage Center
history: The Gubat Heritage Center, established within the historic Casa Escurel-Sabater at the intersection of Quezon and Diaz Streets in Gubat, Sorsogon, serves as an adaptively reused multi-purpose civic asset and lifestyle museum. Originally constructed in 1918 by Don Juan Pura Escurel, a former gobernadorcillo of the municipality, the two-story residential building features a classic American-period interpretation of traditional timber-framed Filipino architecture. Today, the ground floor functions as an active modern art gallery and administrative headquarters for the Municipal Tourism and Cultural Affairs Office (MTCAO), while the second floor serves as a structured lifestyle museum preserving historical artifacts, family memorabilia, and records of the town's prominent 19th-century abaca trading industry.
technical_description: Gubat Heritage Center is a two-storey building constructed in 1918 as a private ancestral family residence and now an LGU-owned multi-purpose cultural, historical, and administrative facility. It stands beside the Almacenes structures. The painted stone masonry walls rise on both storeys beneath a hip roof of painted galvanized iron sheet, while the interior walls, columns, beams, ceiling, floor system, staircase, doors, and window frames are painted timber. The materials are not fully consistent but are generally in good condition despite past storm damage and age. Interventions include replacement of roof members, wall sections, and columns, partial removal of structural components, new window sets, and exterior repainting.

name: Gubat North Central School
history: N/A
technical_description: The one-storey Gabaldon building of Gubat North Central School was built in 1928 as an office and is now used as an office and classroom. It combines a reinforced concrete floor system with painted concrete exterior and interior walls, columns, beams, and staircase beneath a pyramid-hip roof of painted steel. Ceramic tile flooring, a timber ceiling, wooden doors and door frames, and steel window frames complete the structure. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, having undergone crack repairs and concrete patching.

name: Monreal Ruins
history: The Monreal Ruins (officially the Monreal School Building Ruins) in Gubat, Sorsogon, were built from 1904 to 1906 under the guidance of Dr. Bernardino Monreal, the first Filipino civil governor of Sorsogon province. Today, the structurally compromised, unroofed coral walls remain unrestored and are currently off-limits to the general public due to safety concerns.
technical_description: Monreal Ruins is a one-storey former school building built in 1901 and now a historical landmark owned by the LGU, with restricted access and the Gubat Municipal Library adjacent to it. The unpainted structure is made entirely of coral stone and lime, including its exterior and interior walls, columns, floor system, and staircase, and has no roof. It sustained damage from fire, storm, and age in the past. Materials are consistent but not generally in good condition, with cracks, biological growth, and decay observed and no observable interventions recorded.

name: Old Spanish Presidencia
history:
Before its halls welcomed students, the Old Presidencia of Gubat held affairs of the town where it was carried out. Its construction can be traced back to the 1870s with its striking architectural features, use of coral as a construction material, and its strategic location in the town center near the church and plaza, reflect the American and Spanish-era town planning. 
Originally, this structure served as the local municipio of the town, but according to locals, the structure served several purposes over the years. Following the relocation of municipal offices and operations, the building also became a hospital or puericulture center offering urgent medical and maternal services to the residents. After this, the building also held the governmental office of the National Food Authority, managing local agricultural distributions in the municipality. 
In 1996, this building was officially inaugurated as the Bicol University Gubat Campus, completely converting its spaces for academic growth. Throughout the years, this building served the people in many different ways, proving its historical significance and contributions to the culture of Gubat and its people.
technical_description: The Old Spanish Presidencia of Gubat is a two-storey reinforced concrete building, formerly the municipal town hall and now a national government-owned school building beside the Gubat Town Plaza Complex. The record lists its construction as 1996. It has painted concrete exterior and interior walls, columns, beams, ceiling, floor system, and staircase beneath a hip roof of painted steel, with wooden doors and timber window frames. Having sustained flood, storm, and age-related damage, the materials are not fully consistent but are generally in good condition. Interventions include crack repairs, mortar repointing, replacement of roof members, visible RC jacketing, and partial removal of structural components.

name: Irosin Central School
history: During World War II, this Gabaldon Building also served as a detachment site for the Japanese forces, leading to the construction of foxholes surrounding the building and are said to traverse the premises of Irosin Elementary School. According to local accounts of older folks, these foxholes created by the Japanese military extends through the tunnel reaching the military base at Perez Hill.
technical_description: An educational infrastructure situated in Irosin, Sorsogon, featuring standard Gabaldon-type architectural principles optimized for ventilation, natural lighting, and public primary education instruction.

name: Bendillo Ancestral House
history: The Heritage house is owned by Joel Olondris and has been passed down from his mother, Erlinda Bendillo. It is one of the oldest and sturdiest houses in Juban town. The house is made of original wood and features beautiful wood carvings throughout the structure. Interestingly, there have been no restoration efforts undertaken on the house until now.
technical_description: Bendillo Ancestral House is a two-storey residential house located in Juban, Sorsogon, 4703. The privately owned property of Joel Olondris serves as a residence which is partially accessible to the public. The structure features a hip roof configuration resting on timber columns and beams with a timber flooring system throughout both storeys. Exterior walls are painted timber, roofing is painted steel sheet, and doors, window frames, ceiling and staircase are all wood-finished. Materials are consistent throughout, although the assessment notes that the structural materials are generally in good condition wherein roof members appear to have been replaced recently. But surprisingly, other than the restored roof members, there are no recorded restoration efforts taken on the house.

name: Casa Feliz
history: The Casa Feliz, constructed in 1898 along the Maharlika Highway in Juban, Sorsogon, was built as the private residence and district office of Don Leoncio Grajo, Sorsogon’s first representative to the Philippine Assembly. Structurally following the late 19th-century bahay na bato typology, the building consists of a ground floor built from load-bearing stone block masonry coated in traditional lime plaster (paletada), supporting a secondary upper floor constructed from indigenous hardwood. Currently, the infrastructure has undergone adaptive reuse, operating commercially as an 8-room transit lodging inn, event function venue, and outdoor garden café.
technical_description:
Casa Feliz is a two-storey ancestral house topped with a hip roof, featuring painted timber walls and columns, composite beams, and timber floor systems throughout. Its facade displays a marker reading "Casa Feliz Lodging and Function Rooms," while the rear features an azotea with galvanized iron furniture alongside a grand staircase supported by bold concrete colonnets. Other notable details include visible heavy hardwood foundation logs at every corner and a traditional banggera beside a corner window.

Inside, a timber staircase leads up to a small caída (foyer) on the second floor overlooking the main area. The open sala, historically used for hosting prominent guests and large gatherings, flows into a comedor (dining area) built for 12. The interior features painted stone walls, wooden doors, timber window frames, intricately carved hardwood furniture, and a consistent linear pattern across the timber ceilings, walls, and floors. Overall, materials are consistent and in generally good condition, with no observable prior structural interventions.

name: Gorospe Ancestral House
history: Constructed back in 1942, it is one of the few ancestral houses found in Juban, Sorsogon. It was originally owned by Lucio Gorospe, the grandfather of the current owner, Joaquin Jr. Gorospe. Everything in the structure remained in its original state except the front door which was replaced.
technical_description: The two-storey ancestral house of Gorospe’s, situated in Juban, Sorsogon, is one of the heritage houses in the town which was constructed in 1942. The residence is privately owned by Mr. Joaquin Gorospe, Jr. as inherited with his grandfather, Lucio Gorospe. It features a hip roof, painted timber exterior walls with timber columns and floor systems throughout both levels. Beam and staircase are concrete, while interior finishes, doors, and window frames remain timber. The assessed materials were consistent and generally in good condition, with no observable structural interventions recorded.

name: Guevarra Ancestral House
history: Old House owned by Guevarra Family. Originally owned by Judge Pedro Guevarra and wife, Marcela Belon. with a land area of more than 800sqm.
technical_description: Guevara Ancestral House is a two-storey ancestral house, with a land area of more than 800 square meters and is located at Guamil St. Brgy. South Poblacion, Juban, Sorsogon. It is originally owned by Judge Pedro Guevarra and wife, Marcela Belon. The house combines a reinforced concrete ground floor with a timber second floor beneath a hip roof of painted steel. Exterior walls are a mix of timber and concrete, interior walls are wood, and the staircase uses wood, concrete, and mixed materials over a timber floor system. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, having undergone crack repairs and concrete patching.

name: Jose G. Alindogan Elementary School
history: Gabaldon-type school building in North Poblacion, Juban Sorsogon. Constructed back in 1923, originally used as the Juban Central School but on June 17, 1967 it was renamed as Jose G. Alindogan Elementary School through R.A. 4899.
technical_description: The one-storey Gabaldon-type classroom building of Jose G. Alindogan ES was built in 1924. It is a mix of timber and reinforced concrete on its floor system and exterior walls, under a hip roof with a painted timber covering. Concrete columns and staircase support a ceramic tile floor, with timber doors, windows, and ceiling finishes. Materials are consistent and in good condition following a full refurbishment, despite past storm damage. Similar to other preserved Gabaldon buildings, the property also has an added ramp feature for accessibility.

name: Jose G. Alindogan Elementary School Annex
history: The 1924 Gabaldon building saw basic repairs in 2019, followed by a major structural renovation commencing in March 2025 with an expected turnover in June 2026. The neighboring Annex building also required major overhauls following extensive typhoon destruction.
technical_description: The JGAES has another Gabaldon-type building. The one-storey annex building was constructed around 1923 combining timber and reinforced concrete floor materials beneath a painted steel hip-style roof over a painted concrete exterior wall. Concrete columns, staircase, and ramp supports the structure, with timber doors, windows, and ceiling. The materials throughout the building are consistent and are in generally good condition, with flooring previously replaced.

name: Bagatao Island Lighthouse
history:
The Bagatao Island lighthouse is located at the eastern side of the entrance to Sorsogon Bay, Province of Sorsogon. It stands at 29ft (8.8m) white cylindrical white Iron tower situated in the rocky headland that forms the southern point in the western end of the Bagatao Island. It gives a total light elevation of 135ft. (41.1m) which serves to mark the entrance to the bay and assist ships in navigating the bend around Ticao Island, Masbate as they head to San Bernardino Strait and exit into the Pacific Ocean. The construction was undertaken under the Bureau of Lighthouse Construction by the American Government sometime in 1903-1904. The tower was one of the several lighthouse towers bought by Spain from France which was turned over to the Americans. 

The work in Bagatao Island Lighthouse began in January 1904 with the work party consisting of 2 Americans and at least 6-10 Chinese carpenters and about 30 Filipino laborers hired from Manila, on account of difficulty in securing local laborers. The permanent work consisted of the erection of iron tower, frame dwelling for the keepers, a frame kitchen, concrete storehouse, an oil room, a cistern of concrete reinforced with steel, a frame latrine a tripod for a port light and cutting of considerable hardwood lumber for use here and other stations.

Towers made of metal known as Tourelle are prefabricated and manufactured in France and can be easily assembled on site usually supported by metal framework. An example of a Tourelle tower is Bagatao Island Lighthouse. The tower, an iron cylinder 29ft in height, was anchored to its concrete base on the summit rock by anchor bolts 1 meter long. The frame dwelling, measuring 38ft and 2 inches by 37ft and 6 inches, was supported by wooden posts set on concrete pillars. The sixth order flashing light (Fresnel Lens), equipped with both incandescent and an ordinary burner, was first lit on May 15, 1904. A red fixed-port light was also displayed on a tripod to the east of the flashing light. 

The remaining work done by July and August consisted of painting the permanent buildings,
removing temporary structures and cutting timber for use of other stations. After completion, the construction party was brought back to Manila. The total cost of the
lighthouse was Php20,190.30. The Local Government Unit of Magallanes, seeing the
historical significance and tourism potential of both the lighthouse and of the Island of Behia,
is working to preserve the structure and Improve the surrounding areas. With the help of the
administration of Governor Robert "Bobet " Lee Rodrigueza which provided augmentation
funds from the Provincial Government of Sorsogon, a view deck with comfort facilities was
constructed and water plumbing were installed. This new construction commenced in the
first quarter of CY 2017.
technical_description: Bagatao Island Lighthouse is a one-storey lighthouse built in 1904 as a navigational aid and still used as a guide for local fishermen. It is owned by the national government, vacant, and partially accessible, with a keeper's dwelling, storehouse, and oil room adjacent. A reinforced concrete base supports painted pre-fabricated iron and steel walls beneath a domed lantern roof of painted copper sheeting, with steel doors and cast iron window frames. Materials are not consistent but are generally in good condition despite past storm and age damage, although exposed rebar was observed. Interventions include concrete patching, replacement of roof members, installed steel braces, and partial removal of structural components. Data for this structure came from secondary (online) sources.

name: Eduardo Lee Chan Memorial School
history: Eduardo Lee Chan Memorial School, formerly known as Magallanes South Central School, was renamed in honor of Eduardo Lee Chan, a prominent landowner and businessman in the town of Magallanes, Sorsogon. Its premises holds one of the recognized Gabaldon buildings in the province of Sorsogon, that is still partially utilized for academic activities. This Gabaldon building remains erected, adjacent to the modern buildings where the town's offices are located.
technical_description: The one-storey Gabaldon-type building of Eduardo Lee Chan Memorial School stands beside the Magallanes Municipal Hall and is owned by the national government. No construction year was recorded. It has a timber floor system and painted timber exterior walls under a hip roof of painted steel, with wood interior walls, concrete columns, a ceramic tile floor, a timber ceiling, a wooden staircase, and timber doors and window frames. Materials are not fully consistent but are generally in good condition, with no observable interventions recorded.

name: Lee Building
history: Constructed in 1948, the Lee Building is one of the Spanish-American style structures in Magallanes. It is a former ancestral home that housed the family of two former mayors of Magallanes, Sorsogon.
technical_description: Lee Building is a two-storey building constructed in 1948 as a private residence and now used as a commercial building among commercial spaces. It combines a reinforced concrete ground floor with a timber second floor beneath a hip roof of painted steel. Exterior walls are a mix of timber and concrete, interior walls, columns, and beams are concrete, and the floor system combines timber and concrete over a timber-finished ceiling. The staircase is wood, doors are steel, and window frames are timber and steel. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, with no observable interventions recorded.
feature_story:
On the corner of a street in the coastal town of Magallanes, a busy store stands, quite opposite from its original nature, being a house where a prominent family once resided. 
The Lee building is remembered as one of the oldest structures in Magallanes. Locals' accounts reveal that they have remembered the building ever since they were young, and remains strong even now that they are in their middle age. According to the locals, this building existed as a residential space for the Lee family, until such time that the original occupants moved out, and the space was converted into a commercial space now owned by a different family.

name: Inang Elementary School
history: N/A
technical_description: The one-storey Gabaldon-type classroom building of Inang Elementary School was built in 1950. It has a timber floor system and painted timber exterior walls under an open-gable roof of painted steel, with concrete interior walls and columns, a timber ceiling, and timber doors and window frames. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, with flooring previously replaced.

name: Pilar I Central School
history: Constructed in 1914 and put into service by 1920, this Gabaldon building transitioned from holding halls and offices to housing active classrooms. Maintained gradually to preserve its original design, a 2018 repair kept its signature Capiz windows, cacao wood walls, pipe railings, and unaltered concrete columns while replacing decaying wooden board floors with ceramic tiles. Its original crawl space (silong) was cemented over back in 1986 to mitigate sea-level impacts.
technical_description: Pilar I Central School’s Gabaldon building was built in 1914 as a hall and office and is now used as a classroom. It is a one-storey structure with painted timber exterior walls and wood interior walls beneath a box-gable roof of painted steel. Concrete columns and a concrete staircase accompany the ceramic tile floor, timber ceiling, and timber doors and window frames. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, with crack repairs and added pipe railings but no structural refinement, though wood decay and water staining are present.

name: Pilar II Central School
history: Established in 1923, the school site features an old Gabaldon structure originating from 1935 that historically served as classroom space. Having undergone one previous restoration, the building is scheduled for a major second renovation cycle spanning from October 2025 through June 2026.
technical_description: The one-storey Gabaldon building of Pilar II Central School was built in 1935 as a classroom and is now vacant, having been recently restored and awaiting reuse. It combines a reinforced concrete floor system with painted concrete exterior and interior walls under a hip roof of painted steel. Concrete columns and staircase support a ceramic tile floor, with a timber ceiling and timber doors and window frames. Materials are consistent and in good condition following extensive interventions, including crack repairs, mortar repointing, concrete patching, and replacement of wall sections and flooring, with no apparent deterioration observed.

name: Escuela Pia Prieto Diaz
history: The Escuela Pia of Prieto Diaz, constructed during the 19th-century Spanish colonial era, was engineered out of local coral stones and rubblework masonry. Architecturally specified as a single-level Spanish schoolhouse (escuela pia) designed for basic instructional delivery, the building features a load-bearing coral-stone foundation enclosing an integrated classroom space. After sustaining severe roof and wall damage from the onslaught of Super Typhoon Reming in 2006, it underwent a restoration project in 2007. The preserved infrastructure continues its original continuous academic utility today, operating as a heritage classroom building amid modern school facilities.
technical_description: Escuela Pia of Prieto Diaz is a one-storey coral stone building recorded as constructed in 1617, originally a school and now an LGU-owned historical site that is vacant but fully accessible. Its unpainted coral stone walls, columns, beams, door and window openings, floor system, and staircase sit beneath an open-gable roof of painted steel, with a painted timber ceiling. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition despite past flood, storm, and age-related damage. Interventions include crack repairs, mortar repointing, replacement of roof members and wall sections, and installed tie rods.
feature_story:
In Prieto Diaz, a structure was built with local materials and colonial-era design, where education took place long before modern school buildings arose. 
 This building remained actively used as part of a public school, continuously serving its purpose in different periods of Philippine education. Over the years, this building has been adapted as part of the Prieto-Diaz Central School, where it functioned as a hall where conventions are held and as classrooms to accommodate more students. 
 The Local Government Units (LGUs), with the help of private foundations and heritage authorities, remain committed to restoring it to its best condition for continued utility and academic service.

name: Museo Sorsogon
history:
There was a time when entering this building meant leaving freedom behind, but now, this building offers freedom for people to visit the history and heritage of Sorsogon.
 Built in 1916, the former Provincial Jail served as a courthouse and prison until 2019. Now it is home to Museo Sorsogon, where very different stories were lived to tell within the same walls. Beyond the building's transition from a jail to a museum in 2021, its own stories were preserved in its architectural and structural features. The jail spaces, doors, and openings were kept as physical remnants of its former function, while displaying objects and art that combine both the heaviness of its past and the light atmosphere of its present. 
Museo Sorsogon offers a peek into the rich culture and heritage of the whole province of Sorsogon, while allowing its old story to remain visible.
technical_description: Museo Sorsogon, the former Provincial Jail and Courthouse, is a two-storey reinforced concrete building built in 1916 and now a national government-owned museum beside the Provincial Capitol. It has painted concrete exterior and interior walls, columns, beams, ceiling, and staircase beneath a hip roof, with a ceramic tile floor, wooden doors, and steel window frames. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, having undergone crack repairs.

name: Sorsogon National High School Building
history: The Sorsogon National High School Building, formerly known as Sorsogon Provincial High School, was established back in June 24, 1903. During its early infrastructure, classes were conducted in its two-storey semi-concrete building. On November 15, 1941, a massive fire completely destroyed the building. It was then reconstructed in the 1950s to a reinforced concrete two-storey building. On February 15, 2014, another fire destroyed the whole interior of the building. It was then restored and finally reopened back on June 5, 2016, with modern materials.
technical_description: Formerly known as the Sorsogon Provincial High School, its early infrastructure consisted of a two-storey semi-concrete building. After being completely destroyed by a massive fire on November 15, 1941, it was reconstructed in the 1950s into a reinforced concrete two-storey building. Following another interior fire on February 15, 2014, the building was comprehensively restored and reopened on June 5, 2016, utilizing modern structural materials while preserving its historic legacy.

name: Sorsogon East Central School
history: Costructed during the American colonization period. Gabaldon building, raised at least 1.2 meters from the ground. Incorporated capiz shells into its windows just as other Gabaldon buildings.
technical_description: The one-storey Gabaldon building of Sorsogon East Central School was built in 1914 as classrooms and is now used as offices. It is almost entirely timber, with painted timber exterior walls, columns, floor system, ceiling, staircase, doors, and window frames, and plastered wood interior walls beneath an open-gable roof of painted steel. The building sustained earthquakes, storms, and age-related damage in the past. Materials are consistent and generally in good condition, with wood decay and water staining observed and crack repairs as the only intervention.

name: Sorsogon Provincial Capitol
history: Constructed back in 1916, the structure was built with an American Colonial Neo-Classical style but has incorporated the architectural, functional and culutural qualities of Filipino Buildings. Its four grand columns were preserved and the structure underwent restorations and renovations to bring back its original architecture style. It is currently still used as the Sorsogon's Capitol Building that houses government departments.
technical_description: The Sorsogon Provincial Capitol is a two-storey reinforced concrete building built in 1916 as the provincial government offices and still serves as the administrative center. It is LGU-owned and stands beside the Sorsogon museum. The painted concrete exterior and interior walls, columns, beams, ceiling, and staircase sit beneath a flat roof, with a ceramic tile floor and timber doors and window frames. Having sustained flood, storm, and age-related damage, the materials are consistent and generally in good condition. Interventions include crack repairs, replacement of roof members, wall sections, and flooring, visible RC jacketing, and partial removal of structural components.
feature_story:
For decades, the Sorsogon Provincial Capitol displayed its white Neoclassical facade in the center of the changing provincial life. As it continues to provide a space for public life, it also preserves the connection to the past and the highly changing life of the city surrounding it. 
	The Sorsogon Capitol highlights key architectural features through its structural elements that emphasize symmetry and grandeur, inspired by classical Greek and Roman Designs. This can be traced back to the American Colonial Period, when the Neoclassical style is greatly popularized. In 2018, this building was officially recognized through a historical marker granted by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines. It then underwent a major restoration in 2021 that aimed to bring back the building’s original architecture while catering to its modern requirements. 
	From the early years of provincial leadership to the wider growth of the city, this capitol is a stronghold of government, while also serving as a historical gem that people visit, photograph, and pass by as a normal part of Sorsogon’s identity and everyday life.
